January 20,2025

MEMORANDUM FOR: Caleb Vitello

Acting Director U.S.Immigration and Customs Enforcement

Pete R.Flores

Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Commissioner U.S. Customs and Border Protection

FROM: Benjamine C. Huffman Acting Secretary

SUBJECT: Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas

This memorandum addresses Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) enforcement actions in or near areas that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) previously determined require special protection. It is effective immediately. This memorandum supersedes and rescinds Alejandro Mayorkas's October 27, 2021 memorandum entitled, Guidelines for Enforcement Actions in or Near Protected Areas.

terminal_record.title: Vought Ordered CFPB Staff to Stop Work; Court Blocked Further Layoffs
terminal_record.description_short: Vought ordered CFPB staff to stop work on Feb. 10, 2025; a judge blocked more layoffs after over 100 workers had been fired.
terminal_record.description_medium: On February 10, 2025, Acting CFPB Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work. A federal judge later blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had been fired that week. The sources support a work stoppage and workforce reduction effort, but do not substantiate the frozen entry’s claim that all roughly 1,700 employees were fired on February 7.
terminal_record.description_long: On February 10, 2025, CFPB Acting Director Russell Vought ordered bureau employees to stop work, according to the District Court’s later account in NTEU v. Vought. The court said the administration was pursuing measures to dismantle the agency, including firings, funding cuts, contract terminations, office closures and a reduction in force. On February 14, NPR reported that a federal judge blocked additional layoffs after more than 100 workers had already been fired that week. The record therefore describes a serious work stoppage and attempted workforce reduction, not a completed firing of the bureau’s full roughly 1,700-person staff. The original February 7 date is not the date of the stop-work order identified in the opinion, and the sources reviewed do not establish that all pending CFPB cases were halted. The injunction was preliminary while litigation continued; it does not by itself decide every underlying legal question. This correction preserves the CFPB action and its immediate legal response while separating completed events from planned reductions. The supplied claim that the bureau’s closure benefited Trump campaign donors is not supported by the sources cited here and is omitted.

terminal_record.description_short: NPR reported two DOGE employees had accounts on classified nuclear networks; DOE said the accounts were never activated or accessed.
terminal_record.description_medium: An NPR report published April 28, 2025 said two DOGE employees had accounts on classified networks used for nuclear information. The Department of Energy said the accounts had never been activated or accessed. NPR also explained that an account’s presence on a network did not by itself grant access to classified data. The reporting documents an account-creation and oversight concern, not confirmed viewing or extraction of nuclear files.
terminal_record.description_long: On April 28, 2025, NPR reported that two Department of Government Efficiency employees had accounts on classified networks used by the National Nuclear Security Administration and the Defense Department. NPR cited two sources who said the accounts had been present for at least two weeks. The Department of Energy first denied that the employees had accessed the networks, then said the accounts had been created but never activated or accessed. NPR also reported that merely appearing on a network directory would not by itself give an employee access to classified data stored there. The supported event is the creation and listing of the accounts, followed by reporting about them and the department’s explanation. The reporting does not establish that either employee viewed, copied, or otherwise accessed nuclear weapons information. It also does not establish the frozen entry’s claims of an unauthorized file breach, foreign business conflicts, or an immediate federal investigation. This repair narrows the entry to the documented access-control concern and preserves the agency’s response.

The order also directed OPM to issue, within 30 days, guidance about additional position categories agencies should consider recommending for inclusion. It says employees in or applicants for these positions need not personally or politically support the President, but are required to faithfully implement administration policies; failure to do so is grounds for dismissal. These are the signed order’s rules and directions. The accessed document does not establish how many positions were later reclassified, how many employees lost protections, or whether any specific person was dismissed under it. This record describes the enacted policy mechanism, not a completed workforce purge or an asserted list of political enemies.

terminal_record.title: P.L. 119-21 Retains Lawful Permanent Residents on SNAP Eligibility List
terminal_record.description_short: The 2025 law’s SNAP eligibility list expressly includes lawful permanent residents.
terminal_record.description_medium: Public Law 119-21, approved July 4, 2025, rewrote SNAP’s noncitizen eligibility subsection. Its list expressly includes lawful permanent residents, so the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The accessed statutory text does not establish the number affected or verify the supplied note about the existing five-year bar.
terminal_record.description_long: On July 4, 2025, Public Law 119-21 amended section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008, SNAP’s eligibility provision. The amendment lists who may qualify: U.S. citizens or nationals; lawful permanent residents; people granted Cuban and Haitian entrant status; and people lawfully residing under a Compact of Free Association. It also says an individual must be a U.S. resident and a household must otherwise qualify under section 6. Because lawful permanent residents appear expressly in the enacted list, the claim that the law eliminated SNAP eligibility for green-card holders generally is inaccurate. The text does not establish how many people lost eligibility or the effects on food access, and this card makes no numerical impact claim. The supplied research note says a prior five-year bar continues to apply to some lawful permanent residents, but I did not verify that detail in the text accessed here, so it is excluded from the asserted description. The source resolves the title’s blanket statement; it does not by itself establish every category that lost eligibility compared with prior law.

source_fact_map.fact: Section 10108 addresses alien SNAP eligibility and amends Food and Nutrition Act section 6(f).
source_fact_map.quote: SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt:
SEC. 10108. ALIEN SNAP ELIGIBILITY.

    Section 6(f) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 (7 U.S.C. 
2015(f)) is amended to read as follows:
    ``(f) No individual who is a member of a household otherwise 
eligible to participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
under this section shall be eligible to participate in the supplemental 
nutrition assistance program as a member of that or any other household 
unless he or she is--
            ``(1) a resident of the United States; and
            ``(2) either--
                    ``(A) a citizen or national of the United States;
                    ``(B) an alien lawfully admitted for permanent 
                residence as an immigrant as defined by sections 
                101(a)(15) and 101(a)(20) of the Immigration and 
                Nationality Act, excluding, among others, alien 
                visitors, tourists, diplomats, and students who enter 
                the United States temporarily with no intention of 
                abandoning their residence in a foreign country;
                    ``(C) an alien who has been granted the status of 
                Cuban and Haitian entrant, as defined in section 501(e) 
                of the Refugee Education Assistance Act of 1980 (Public 
                Law 96-422); or
                    ``(D) an individual who lawfully resides in the 
                United States in accordance with a Compact of Free 
                Association referred to in section 402(b)(2)(G) of the 
                Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity 
                Reconciliation Act of 1996.
        The income (less, at State option, a pro rata share) and 
        financial resources of the individual rendered ineligible to 
        participate in the supplemental nutrition assistance program 
        under this subsection shall be considered in determining the 
        eligibility and the value of the allotment of the household of 
        which such individual is a member.''.

source_claim_snapshot.title: Trump Claims He 'Saved the Economy' with Tariffs Despite Every Major Economist Disagreeing
source_claim_snapshot.synopsis: Throughout May 2025, Trump publicly claimed that his tariff policy had 'saved' the American economy despite near-universal condemnation from mainstream economists, business leaders, and international institutions. The IMF, World Bank, and major economic research organizations all projected the tariffs would reduce US GDP and raise consumer prices. Trump selectively cited cherry-picked data while ignoring the broader picture of market turmoil and credit downgrades. The disconnect between Trump's claims and economic reality exemplified his administration's relationship with facts.

That company-specific statement is distinct from the asserted claim about saving the national economy and cannot verify it. This draft therefore attributes the original allegation to the supplied record, removes the absolute assertion that every major economist disagreed, and does not present the quote or economic effects as established. terminal_record.description_short: The CARES Act temporarily raised the business-interest deduction limit, a change tax advisers said could benefit highly leveraged firms, including private-equity funds.
terminal_record.description_medium: Congress.gov lists the CARES Act as Public Law 116-136, signed March 27, 2020, and says Section 2306 increased the business-interest deduction limit for 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service and Holland & Knight explain that the cap rose from 30% to 50%; tax advisers said this could help leveraged businesses and private-equity funds. terminal_record.description_long: On March 27, 2020, the CARES Act became Public Law 116-136. Section 2306 temporarily raised the cap on deductible business interest from 30 percent to 50 percent for tax years 2019 and 2020. Congressional Research Service explained that the amendment also let firms use 2019 income when calculating the 2020 cap. Holland & Knight’s April 2020 tax analysis said additional deductions could reduce cash taxes or create or increase net operating losses for highly leveraged businesses, including private-equity funds and their portfolio companies. This supports a narrow description of the law’s tax treatment of borrowing costs and its potential benefit to leveraged firms. The sources do not establish the frozen entry’s $1.5 billion estimate, lobbyist authorship, or claim that the provision was inserted without committee scrutiny. Those allegations are omitted rather than treated as facts. The card describes an enacted, broadly applicable tax rule and does not infer that private equity alone received it or that the change produced a particular realized benefit.

terminal_record.title: Trump promoted a $59.99 branded Bible; $300 million in revenue is unsupported
terminal_record.description_short: Trump promoted the $59.99 God Bless the USA Bible; AP reporting does not substantiate the $300 million revenue claim.
terminal_record.description_medium: On March 26, 2024, Trump promoted the God Bless the USA Bible and urged supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. AP later reported close to 120,000 copies shipped to the United States from China by late March and estimated about $7 million in potential retail sales at the minimum price. AP also cited a disclosure showing $300,000 in CIC Ventures Bible royalties, while noting the period and any additional payments were unclear. The $300 million revenue claim is unsupported by these reports.
terminal_record.description_long:
On March 26, 2024, Donald Trump promoted the “God Bless the USA Bible,” urging supporters to buy it from a website listing the price at $59.99. The website said Trump’s name and image were used under a paid license from CIC Ventures, a company he reported owning. The book combined a King James Version Bible with U.S. founding documents and the Pledge of Allegiance.

The original title’s $300 million revenue figure is not substantiated by the reporting reviewed here. In October 2024, the Associated Press reported that trade records showed close to 120,000 copies shipped from China to the United States between early February and late March. At the minimum retail price, AP estimated potential sales revenue for those shipments at about $7 million. AP also cited a financial disclosure showing $300,000 in Bible royalties earned by CIC Ventures, while stating that the disclosure period and any additional payments were unclear. Shipment estimates, potential retail sales, company royalties, and Trump’s total receipts are different measures; these reports do not establish total eventual sales or payments. The corrected entry records the promotion and licensing arrangement, removes the unsupported $300 million claim, and leaves final revenue and total royalties unknown.

terminal_record.description_long: The Department of Education announced a reduction in force on March 11, 2025. Its release said the action would affect nearly 50 percent of the department’s workforce and that impacted staff would be placed on administrative leave beginning March 21. The department listed 4,133 employees when President Trump took office and roughly 2,183 after the action; it said nearly 600 employees had already accepted voluntary resignation or retirement opportunities during the prior seven weeks. ABC News reported that reduction-in-force notices went to 1,315 employees on March 11 and that those affected were set to enter administrative leave on March 21, with pay and benefits through June 9. The department described the action as part of its “final mission.” This repaired account records the department’s announced workforce reduction and reported scale. The sources do not establish that DOGE directly ordered or carried out the reduction, so the frozen card’s DOGE attribution is omitted. terminal_record.title: Trump Issues Harvard Entry Suspension; Current Visa Revocations Remain Under Consideration
terminal_record.description_short: A June 4 proclamation suspended entry for some incoming Harvard students and only called for discretionary review of current visas.
terminal_record.description_medium: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump issued a proclamation suspending entry for certain nonimmigrant students seeking to begin study at Harvard through SEVP, with exceptions and a stated six-month duration. It separately directed the Secretary of State to consider whether some current Harvard students’ visas should be revoked. That instruction did not establish that current students’ visas had already been canceled. A later temporary court order blocked the policy, according to Harvard Gazette.
terminal_record.description_long: On June 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a proclamation suspending entry for nonimmigrants seeking to begin a course of study at Harvard through the Student and Exchange Visitor Program. The proclamation set a six-month period unless extended and included exceptions; it also said the restriction did not apply to students entering to attend other universities through the program. Separately, it directed the Secretary of State to consider, in the Secretary’s discretion, whether certain current Harvard students with F, M, or J visas should have them revoked. That wording authorized a review; it does not say that visas belonging to dozens of current students had already been canceled. The proclamation stated national-security concerns and alleged Harvard had failed to provide records about foreign students. Harvard Gazette reported that University officials denied that allegation and that DHS had moved in May to pull Harvard’s certification. The Gazette also reported a temporary court order issued June 5 blocking the administration’s plan. This supported entry covers the June 4 proclamation and separates it from the earlier certification dispute and April SEVIS record terminations. The number of students affected by those separate actions remains unresolved.

terminal_record.description_long: After Serena Williams’ 2009 U.S. Open semifinal against Kim Clijsters ended in a point penalty following a dispute with a line judge, Trump wrote a blog response defending Williams against public criticism. Sportskeeda quotes him saying, “The backlash against Serena has been relentless and she has been treated badly. She has apologized and I think enough is enough.” The same report says he argued that Williams should be allowed to move on and that the line judge should apologize; a separate account by HITC reproduces those remarks. The reporting contradicts this entry’s original claim that Trump called Williams ugly, a bad person, or bad at golf. This corrected record describes the supported event: Trump’s defense of Williams in response to criticism following the 2009 match. The source accounts do not establish the exact publication date of the original Trump University blog post or the number of people who read it. The frozen August date is also incorrect for the U.S. Open incident, which took place in September 2009.

terminal_record.title: Trump Uses “Animals” Remark During California Immigration Roundtable
terminal_record.description_short: Trump Used “Animals” Remark During May 2018 California Immigration Roundtable
terminal_record.description_medium: At a May 16, 2018, White House roundtable on sanctuary-city policies, President Donald Trump said, “These aren’t people. These are animals” after Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member she could not report to ICE. Trump’s reply referred broadly to “people coming into the country” without naming a group. The White House and Trump later said he meant MS-13; FactCheck.org said the original remark’s intended target could not be established with certainty.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 16, 2018, President Donald Trump held a White House roundtable with California mayors, sheriffs and other officials about sanctuary-city policies. During the discussion, Fresno County Sheriff Margaret Mims said she knew of an MS-13 member but could not tell ICE unless that person met a threshold. Trump replied that “people coming into the country” were “animals,” saying, “These aren’t people. These are animals.” In the official transcript, the remark immediately follows Mims’s reference to MS-13, but Trump’s reply does not name the gang. The White House press secretary later said Trump was referring to MS-13 gang members, and Trump said the next day that he meant MS-13. FactCheck.org reported those explanations while noting that it could not determine exactly what Trump meant in the original remark. The record should therefore describe the words and their immediate setting, then attribute the later clarification separately. It should not say the transcript proves that Trump was referring to all immigrants, or that it definitively proves he meant only MS-13. The sources establish the public remark and context; they do not document a resulting policy change or quantify harm caused by it.

terminal_record.description_short: Trump said a major Istanbul building gave him “a little conflict of interest” when discussing Turkey in a 2015 interview.
terminal_record.description_medium: In a December 1, 2015 interview on Breitbart News Daily, Donald Trump said he had “a little conflict of interest” because of a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. This supports a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not establish repeated Turkish-government bookings at the Istanbul property or that the business interest shaped U.S. policy toward Turkey.
terminal_record.description_long: On December 1, 2015, Donald Trump spoke on Breitbart News Daily about Turkey and said he had “a little conflict of interest” because he had a major building in Istanbul called Trump Towers. TIME later quoted the remark and identified it as a 2015 interview; Politico reported on a Tuesday-morning Breitbart interview on December 1, 2015. The statement documents a public acknowledgment of a potential business conflict while discussing Turkey. It does not show that Turkish government agencies or affiliated groups booked Trump Towers Istanbul during his presidency, that those bookings generated payments to Trump, or that U.S. decisions toward Turkey were made to benefit the property. The held record further alleges that Trump repeatedly favored President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan because of this business interest. The sources accessed for this repair do not establish that causal link. This account therefore records the 2015 statement and leaves the broader booking and policy-influence allegations unresolved; it does not present them as findings of corruption or proof that the property changed government policy.

proposed_survivor_patch.description_medium: During the January 2017 inauguration, the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee booked rooms, meals and event space at Trump International Hotel in Washington. WNYC and ProPublica reported internal emails and receipts documenting payments and a dispute over event-space pricing. The report said the final rental price was unclear.
proposed_survivor_patch.description_long: During the January 2017 inauguration, the 58th Presidential Inaugural Committee booked rooms, meals and event space at Trump International Hotel in Washington. In December 2018, WNYC and ProPublica reported on interviews, internal emails and receipts documenting the committee’s payments to the Trump Organization and a dispute over event-space pricing. The hotel’s managing director offered $175,000 per day for ballroom and meeting-room use, or $700,000 for four days. An inaugural planner questioned the proposed rates, and the article said it was unclear what amount the committee ultimately paid for the rental. This evidence documents a commercial relationship and a pricing concern; it does not establish the Trump Organization’s net profit, a hundreds-of-thousands amount earned during inauguration weekend, or a final determination that the prices violated law. A separate D.C. attorney general complaint filed in 2020 alleged overpayment for event space, but its allegations belong to a later lawsuit record and are not proof of the frozen row’s weekend-profit claim. The event description should remain limited to payments and price negotiations documented in the reporting.

terminal_record.title: ProPublica Reported GOP Committees Spent at Trump Properties; RNC Said Rates Were Market
terminal_record.description_short: ProPublica documented political committee spending at Trump properties; an RNC official said the properties charged market rates.
terminal_record.description_medium: ProPublica’s May 2018 analysis of Federal Election Commission filings reported at least $3.1 million in political committee spending at Trump Organization properties since the 2016 election. It listed at least $945,027 in Republican National Committee spending, mostly for fundraising and political-event venues. An anonymous RNC official said the properties charged market rates. The reporting supports the spending and conflict context, not the frozen claim that committees generally paid above-market rates.
terminal_record.description_long: On May 4, 2018, ProPublica reported that political committees had spent at least $3.1 million at Trump Organization properties since the 2016 presidential election, based on expenditure reports submitted to the Federal Election Commission. It said the vast majority of that spending came from Republican-connected committees. ProPublica listed at least $1,684,700 in post-election spending by Donald J. Trump for President and at least $945,027 by the Republican National Committee, mostly for fundraising and political-event venues. An anonymous RNC official told ProPublica that the properties charged the committee market rates. These records support a narrower account of political committees directing reported spending to properties owned by the president’s company while he held office. They do not support the frozen entry’s allegation that committees generally paid above-market prices or its claim of tens of millions in such payments. The market-rate statement is an attributed defense, not an independent price comparison. ProPublica also notes that its dataset covered electronic FEC filings and excluded some committees that filed on paper, so the figures are not a complete count of all political spending.
terminal_record.date_basis: The source reports spending since the 2016 election and was published May 4, 2018; this is the reported period, not a verified first transaction date.

terminal_record.description_long: On March 27, 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the State Department may have revoked more than 300 visas. He described the total as including student and visitor visas and said he had signed each action. He made the remarks in Guyana after federal agents detained Tufts University doctoral student Rumeysa Ozturk and the State Department revoked her visa. The Associated Press reported that Ozturk's lawyer said no charges had been filed. AP also reported that she was one of four students who wrote a Tufts Daily opinion piece criticizing the university's response to demands for divestment from companies tied to Israel. Reuters reported Rubio did not explain what specific conduct by Ozturk justified revoking her visa. He listed vandalism, harassment, building takeovers and other disruptive conduct as grounds for taking away student visas, but did not say Ozturk had done those things. He said the standard in her case involved support for movements contrary to U.S. foreign policy. The reporting does not show that every visa in the reported total was revoked for criticism of Israel, for a social media post, or for one common reason; it leaves individual grounds unresolved.

terminal_record.title: CBP's Electronic-Device Search Policy Predates the 2025 Claim
terminal_record.description_short: DHS announced electronic-media border-search directives in 2009; the record does not establish a February 2025 expansion.
terminal_record.description_medium: DHS announced directives governing searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry in August 2009. The eCFR separately defines “reasonable distance” for immigration officers as within 100 air miles of a U.S. external boundary, and a 2008 ACLU report traces that regulation to 1953. These sources establish a preexisting framework, not a February 2025 Trump action ending Fourth Amendment protections or expanding device searches. The claimed thousands of court challenges remain unsupported.
terminal_record.description_long: On August 27, 2009, the Department of Homeland Security announced directives for searches of computers and other electronic media at U.S. ports of entry. DHS described the policy as consistent with its border authority over non-electronic materials. Separately, the eCFR defines “reasonable distance” under section 287(a)(3) of the Immigration and Nationality Act as within 100 air miles from an external boundary, while a 2008 ACLU report says the regulation establishing the 100-mile zone was adopted in 1953. These sources show that electronic-media border-search guidance and the 100-mile immigration regulation predate the alleged February 2025 policy. They do not establish that Trump ended Fourth Amendment protections, expanded an electronic-device search zone in February 2025, or caused thousands of court challenges. The frozen entry also combines the statutory operating distance for immigration officers with electronic-device searches; the accessed material does not show that the two authorities are interchangeable. This replacement narrows the card to the documented policy background and leaves the claimed 2025 action unsupported.

terminal_record.title: Lawsuit Alleges ICE Shared Iranian Asylum Seekers’ Immigration Files with Iran
terminal_record.description_short: A 2026 lawsuit alleges that U.S. officials shared Iranian asylum seekers’ confidential immigration files with Iran beginning in March 2025; DHS denies it.
terminal_record.description_medium: A July 2026 complaint by the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund alleges that the Trump administration adopted a policy in March 2025 to give Iran confidential immigration-file information about Iranian asylum seekers. The complaint says ICE and Iranian officials held monthly meetings to share records. CNN reported the suit and quoted a DHS spokesperson denying the allegation. These are allegations, not court findings; the complaint seeks declaratory and injunctive relief.
terminal_record.description_long: On July 7, 2026, the Iranian American Legal Defense Fund filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia through Public Citizen. The complaint alleges that the Trump administration adopted a policy in March 2025 to provide the Iranian government with confidential immigration-file information about Iranians seeking asylum in the United States. It says ICE and Iranian officials held monthly meetings to share records of people in ICE custody and that officials also sent or hand-delivered files. The complaint alleges that hundreds of Iranian detainees seeking asylum were affected and argues that disclosure could endanger applicants and relatives; those claims have not been adjudicated. CNN reported the complaint and quoted a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson saying the allegations that ICE shared asylum application records with Iran were false. The complaint asks the court for declaratory and injunctive relief, so no finding of unlawful sharing or resulting persecution is established here. The evidence is limited to Iranian asylum seekers and the Iranian government. The supplied date of March 1 is only a month-level anchor: the complaint says March 2025, not a specific day. The broader frozen claim about sharing detailed information with multiple foreign governments and documented targeting cases is not supported by these sources and is excluded.
